Devlore is a documentation tool that watches the GitHub repos you connect to it and keeps their documentation current automatically, without anyone having to write it by hand. Every push to a linked repo gets a draft summary of what changed and why; every release tag folds those drafts into reviewed, official reference docs. Once a project has some history, you can ask Devlore questions about it directly — why a decision was made, what a piece of code does, what changed in a given release — through a small local chat interface that never sends your code or your Anthropic API key anywhere except Anthropic's own API.

It's built for anyone working on a codebase who wants documentation to stay honest as the code moves, whether that's a solo developer, a future collaborator picking up someone else's project, or a team where the person who understood a decision has since moved on.

## Getting Started with the Setup Wizard
<!-- requirements: #14, #15, #16, #20, #27, #28 -->

Devlore runs as a small local server plus a browser tab, not a hosted service — everything happens on your own machine using your own accounts and your own Anthropic API key. The first time you open Devlore, a guided setup wizard walks you through connecting it to GitHub step by step, rather than asking you to edit repo settings by hand.

The wizard starts by asking for a GitHub personal access token, with a direct link to GitHub's token-creation page and the exact permissions to grant. Paste the token into the wizard's own field — it's sent straight to Devlore's local server and used to talk to GitHub's API; it's never typed anywhere else, and never handed to Claude. Request the token with access to "All repositories" in your account, since that's what lets you link additional repos later without repeating this step or re-scoping the token.

Next, the wizard checks whether your GitHub account already has a vault — a dedicated repo named `devlore-vault` that holds every linked project's drafted documentation. If one doesn't exist yet, the wizard creates it for you (private by default, since it holds your projects' history, not something meant to be public). If you're reinstalling Devlore, or running it on a second machine under the same GitHub account, the wizard finds and reuses your existing vault instead of creating a second one.

Once the token and vault are set up, this is a one-time step — you won't need to go through it again to link another project.

[↑ Back to table of contents](#table-of-contents)

## Linking an Existing Project
<!-- requirements: #22 -->

To connect a repo you already have, choose "Link a project" and pick the repo. Devlore checks it first: if it's never been linked before, it proceeds with the normal setup; if it's already linked, it tells you whether the existing setup matches what the current version of Devlore expects. If everything's current, there's nothing to do. If Devlore's own workflow files have changed since you linked, you'll see an "out of date" notice with the choice to update — Devlore never overwrites anything without you asking it to.

Linking writes two small workflow files into the project repo and provisions the secrets they need (your Anthropic API key and a vault-write token) automatically — you never need to hand-edit YAML or repo settings yourself. Once linked, every future push to that repo starts routing through Devlore on its own.

[↑ Back to table of contents](#table-of-contents)

## Creating a New Project
<!-- requirements: #21 -->

Choose "Create a new project" to have Devlore create a brand-new private GitHub repo for you rather than linking one that already exists. Enter a name; if that name is already taken in your account, the wizard tells you immediately and lets you pick a different one — it never fails with a raw error or silently reuses the existing repo. Once the name is confirmed, Devlore creates the repo, sets up the same workflow files and secrets a linked repo gets, and seeds it with a starter `docs/PRODUCT.md` to get you started.

[↑ Back to table of contents](#table-of-contents)

## Your Project's docs/PRODUCT.md
<!-- requirements: #33, #18 -->

`docs/PRODUCT.md` is your project's own living design document — its intent, decisions, and requirements, written in your own words. Devlore treats its *path* as protected (it must stay at exactly that location for Devlore to find it) but never touches its *content* — it's yours to write and edit freely, including as grounding material when brainstorming with an AI coding assistant.

When you link or create a project, Devlore checks for this file. If it's missing, Devlore creates a starter template for you, with a small banner explaining the convention. If one already exists and carries Devlore's marker, it's left alone. If one exists but predates Devlore — hand-written, or written by another tool — the wizard flags this before proceeding: you can cancel, or have Claude propose a reorganized version matching the starter template's shape. You'll always see that proposal as a preview first; nothing is written until you explicitly confirm it.

Every time you push to a linked project, Devlore also mirrors the current content of your `docs/PRODUCT.md` into its vault, so the chat interface can ground answers like "why did we require X" in your project's own actual design doc, not just what Devlore has drafted on its own.

[↑ Back to table of contents](#table-of-contents)

## Unlinking a Project
<!-- requirements: #32 -->

If you no longer want a project routed through Devlore, open its entry and choose to unlink it. Unlinking removes the workflow files and secrets from that project's own repo, so no further pushes trigger Devlore for it. Separately, you're asked whether you also want to delete that project's accumulated history from the vault, or keep it as a historical record even though the project is no longer actively linked — this defaults to "keep," since deleting history can't be undone. One exception: if the project's own GitHub repo has already been deleted outside Devlore, there's no repo left to detach from, so the vault-deletion checkbox defaults to checked instead, with an explanation — otherwise unlinking a deleted repo would do nothing visible at all.

[↑ Back to table of contents](#table-of-contents)

## Exploring Your Linked Projects
<!-- requirements: #36, #39, #41 -->

The home view is what you land on before picking a project or opening the wizard — a short summary of what Devlore does, plus three clickable squares: Create a new project, Link an existing project, and Explore linked projects. Clicking Create or Link jumps straight into the setup wizard already switched to that mode. Clicking Explore expands the sidebar's project list and shows an explore pane in the main area.

The left rail's project sublist starts collapsed on a fresh page load, so you're not shown the full list before asking for it — click "Explore linked projects" to expand it. The whole left rail can also be collapsed down to icons only, using the chevron toggle at its top, if you want more room for the main content; your choice is remembered the next time you open Devlore.

[↑ Back to table of contents](#table-of-contents)

## What Happens When You Push Code
<!-- requirements: #1, #2, #3, #17, #46 -->

Once a project is linked, every push you make to it is picked up automatically — no extra step on your part. Devlore diffs the push against what it last saw, and drafts a log entry describing what changed and why, based on the diff and the project's current documentation. This happens with no approval needed; it's a running draft trail, not the official record, and it's stored in the vault, not in your project's own repo.

Before anything is sent to Claude, Devlore redacts anything that looks like a secret — API keys, tokens, private keys, and similarly-named files (`.env`, `.pem`, credentials files, and so on) are stripped or replaced with a placeholder. This applies to every diff, on every push, with no action needed from you.

Occasionally, a push represents more than a routine change — a real fork in the road where one approach was chosen over genuine alternatives (a technology or architecture choice, a reversed decision, a dependency adopted or dropped, a convention established). When Devlore judges a push to clear that bar, it also drafts a short decision record alongside the ordinary log entry, so "why did we choose X" has a dedicated, curated answer later instead of being buried in routine history.

[↑ Back to table of contents](#table-of-contents)

## Cutting a Release
<!-- requirements: #4, #5, #42 -->

When you push a release tag (in the form `v1.2.3`), two things happen automatically. First, Devlore reads every draft log entry since the previous release plus the project's current official docs, and drafts an update to those official docs — but instead of committing it directly, it opens a pull request in the vault repo. A person with approval rights reviews and merges (or edits) that pull request; this is the one point in the whole workflow where a human is deliberately in the loop, since master documentation is meant to stay accurate on an ongoing basis.

Second, Devlore drafts release notes scoped to just that release — a plain-language, user-facing summary of what changed since the previous tag, distinct from the more durable master docs. Release notes are committed straight into the vault with no review step, since they're pinned to an already-cut, immutable release rather than something that needs ongoing accuracy.

[↑ Back to table of contents](#table-of-contents)

## Asking Questions in the Documentation Chat
<!-- requirements: #23, #46, #47 -->

The "Documentation chat" tab lets you ask a linked project questions in plain language — "why did we switch to Postgres in March," "what does this repo actually do," "why did we choose this approach over that one." Pick a project from the sidebar first; each question is scoped to that one project's documentation, so answers stay grounded and don't mix content from unrelated projects.

Devlore draws on everything it's automatically generated about the project — its draft log entries, decision records, master docs, product doc, and more — to answer. Replies render as formatted text (headings, lists, code blocks), not raw markdown.

Asking a question can take a little while, since it involves refreshing the project's documentation and then waiting on Claude's actual response — the chat shows a running timer for each phase so a long wait reads as "still working," not "stuck." If a reply is taking unusually long, the message escalates to "Still waiting on Claude…" with a Cancel button, so you're never left staring at an indefinite wait with no way out. If a request fails because GitHub or Claude is having a genuine, ongoing outage, the error message says so, rather than suggesting your own setup is broken.

[↑ Back to table of contents](#table-of-contents)

## Keeping the Vault Synced
<!-- requirements: #30, #31 -->

Devlore's local chat server reads from its own synced copy of your vault, refreshed automatically every time you launch the app. Beyond that, a "Vault settings" panel lets you choose how it stays current: refresh before every chat question (the default — favors always-current answers over a bit of extra wait), or refresh on a timer at an interval you set between 1 and 60 minutes. In timer mode, a manual "Refresh now" button is available for those moments you've just pushed and want an answer immediately without waiting for the next tick; in per-query mode that button is hidden, since every question already refreshes on its own. If a refresh ever fails — you're offline, a rate limit, an expired token — Devlore shows you what happened and answers your next question against whatever it already has locally, rather than blocking you entirely.

[↑ Back to table of contents](#table-of-contents)

## Tracking Token Usage
<!-- requirements: #24 -->

Each project's entry in the left rail shows two running totals: how many tokens its automatic documentation drafting has used, and how many tokens your own chat questions about it have used. Both figures update live after every chat reply. There's no dollar figure shown alongside them — Anthropic doesn't expose current pricing through its API, so Devlore only shows raw token counts rather than a cost estimate that could silently drift out of date.

## Reading the User Manual
<!-- requirements: #38 -->

This document — a task-oriented guide to actually using the product — is available inside the app itself, not just as a file in a repo. Open it from the "User Manual" toggle in the left rail; it opens alongside whatever else you're looking at, rather than covering it, so you can read instructions and keep working at the same time. Internal links within the manual, like the ones at the end of each section here, smooth-scroll to the right place instead of leaving the page. The manual you see in the app always describes Devlore itself, regardless of which of your own linked projects you currently have selected.

[↑ Back to table of contents](#table-of-contents)

## Unlocking the Visualizer, Test Plan, and Release Notes
<!-- requirements: #45 -->

Three tabs — Visualizer, Test plan, and Release notes — are part of Devlore's paid tier. They're always visible and clickable; if you haven't unlocked them yet, clicking one shows an explanation of what that tab does instead of its real content, along with a button to unlock it. A matching "Unlock features" link sits in the left rail, underneath "Support Devlore" — using either one flips your unlocked status immediately, and whichever gated tab you have open re-renders right away to reflect it.

[↑ Back to table of contents](#table-of-contents)

## Visualizing Your Project's Architecture
<!-- requirements: #12 -->

The Visualizer tab shows diagrams of how a project fits together — relationships within the repo, between the repo and any APIs it calls, and across your other linked projects. Diagrams are generated automatically and refresh as a project's requirements change; there's nothing to manually trigger. Each diagram sits in its own zoomable viewport: scroll to zoom, drag to pan, or use the on-diagram +/− and reset controls, which matters once a diagram has more than a handful of nodes and would otherwise be too small to read.

[↑ Back to table of contents](#table-of-contents)

## Generating and Reading a QA Test Plan
<!-- requirements: #35 -->

The Test plan tab holds a manual QA test plan for the selected project, generated from that project's own `docs/PRODUCT.md` requirements. It's fully machine-owned — regenerated automatically whenever the requirements change, so there's no manual step to keep it current, and any hand-edits to the file itself won't survive the next regeneration. Cases are grouped by feature area, one case per distinct observable behavior, each traceable back to the requirement number it covers; anything described as not yet built shows up in a separate out-of-scope section rather than being tested as if it already existed.

[↑ Back to table of contents](#table-of-contents)

## Reviewing Release Notes
<!-- requirements: #43 -->

The Release notes tab lists every release Devlore has drafted for the selected project, most recent first. Each entry is the plain-language summary produced automatically when that release's tag was pushed — what changed since the previous release, written for someone using the product rather than someone reading commit history. If nothing's been released yet, the tab shows an explanatory empty state instead of blank space.

[↑ Back to table of contents](#table-of-contents)

## Supporting Devlore
<!-- requirements: -->

If Devlore is useful to you, a "Support Devlore" link in the left rail (and in the settings menu) leads to a Ko-fi page where you can leave a one-time donation. It's entirely optional and has no effect on anything else in the app.
